title: DNS & CoreDNS
summary: How Services and Pods get DNS names, how Pods search them, how CoreDNS is configured, and how to debug DNS with a test Pod.

blocks.text: Kubernetes creates DNS records for **Services and Pods**, so clients can use stable names instead of IPs. The kubelet configures each Pod's DNS.

rows: The IPs of all selected Pods
Port number plus a domain name

blocks.text: For a headless Service, the SRV query returns one answer per backing Pod, using the Pod's `hostname.my-svc.my-namespace.svc...` name.
An unqualified name is looked up in the **Pod's own namespace**. The kubelet writes each Pod's `/etc/resolv.conf`, and its `search` list expands short names:

nameserver <cluster-dns-ip>
search <namespace>.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5

items: A Pod in namespace `test` looking up `data` will not find Service `data` in namespace `prod`.
`data.prod` or `data.prod.svc.cluster.local` both work from `test`.
Limits: at most **32** search domains, or **2048** characters across all of them.
Pod A record form: `<pod-IPv4-address>.<namespace>.pod.<cluster-domain>` with dots in the IP turned into dashes, e.g. `172-17-0-3.default.pod.cluster.local`.
A Pod's hostname is its `metadata.name` unless `spec.hostname` is set.
With `spec.hostname: foo` and `spec.subdomain: bar` in `my-namespace`, the FQDN is `foo.bar.my-namespace.svc.cluster.local`.
DNS only serves records for that FQDN if a **headless Service named like the subdomain** exists in the same namespace.
The Pod must be ready to get a record, unless the Service sets `publishNotReadyAddresses`.
`setHostnameAsFQDN: true` makes `hostname` return the full FQDN (max 64 characters, or the Pod won't start).

rows: Use cluster DNS; names outside the cluster domain go upstream
Inherit name resolution from the node
Use for `hostNetwork: true` Pods that still need cluster DNS
Ignore Kubernetes DNS settings; everything comes from `dnsConfig`

blocks.text: "Default" is **not** the default. If `dnsPolicy` is unset, `ClusterFirst` applies. A `hostNetwork` Pod left on ClusterFirst falls back to Default behaviour.
`dnsConfig` works with any policy and is required with `None`. Fields: `nameservers` (up to 3 IPs), `searches`, and `options` (name plus optional value, e.g. `ndots`).

items: CoreDNS's Service is named **kube-dns** for compatibility with the legacy kube-dns name.
The kubelet tells containers the DNS server with `--cluster-dns=<dns-service-ip>` and the domain with `--cluster-domain=<default-local-domain>`.
Configuration lives in the **Corefile**, stored in ConfigMap `coredns` in namespace `kube-system`.
After editing the ConfigMap, the `reload` plugin applies it; allow about two minutes.

rows: Answers queries for Service and Pod records in `cluster.local`
Frontend cache (`cache 30` in the default Corefile)
Log errors, halt on forwarding loops, auto-reload, randomize record order

blocks.text: A **stub domain** is an extra server block that forwards one domain to its own nameserver:

items: CoreDNS is the **default** cluster DNS implementation; it's a CNCF-hosted project.
When you upgrade with kubeadm, it keeps your existing Corefile automatically.
When upgrading CoreDNS manually, make sure to keep your Corefile.

blocks.text:
kubectl apply -f https://k8s.io/examples/admin/dns/dnsutils.yaml
kubectl exec -i -t dnsutils -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl exec -ti dnsutils -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl get pods --namespace=kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl logs --namespace=kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl get svc --namespace=kube-system
kubectl get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=kube-dns --namespace=kube-system

items: CoreDNS Pods carry the label `k8s-app=kube-dns` (kept for compatibility).
To see each query, add the `log` plugin: `kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap coredns`.
CoreDNS needs list/watch on Services and EndpointSlices; check `kubectl describe clusterrole system:coredns`.
Service in another namespace? Query `<service-name>.<namespace>`.
Ubuntu's systemd-resolved can cause a forwarding loop; point the kubelet's `--resolv-conf` at `/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf` (kubeadm does this automatically).

blocks.text: Check DNS from a throwaway Pod with `kubectl exec -i -t dnsutils -- nslookup <service-name>.<namespace>`. If it fails, check in order: resolv.conf, CoreDNS Pods, logs, the kube-dns Service, then its EndpointSlices.

questions.stem: Service web lives in namespace shop and the cluster domain is cluster.local. What is its FQDN?

options.explanation: Form: <service>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>.
The Service name comes before the namespace.
The pod label is for Pod records; Services use svc.
svc comes after the namespace.

questions.stem: A Pod in namespace test runs nslookup data. Service data exists only in namespace prod. What happens?

options.text: No result; the short name is searched in the Pod's own namespace
options.explanation: Queries without a namespace are limited to the Pod's namespace.

options.text: It resolves to data in prod
options.explanation: You need data.prod for another namespace.

options.text: It resolves to the first matching Service in any namespace
options.explanation: DNS doesn't search all namespaces.

questions.stem: If dnsPolicy is not set on a Pod, the policy named "Default" is used.

options.explanation: The default is ClusterFirst; "Default" means inherit from the node.
Correct. ClusterFirst is used when dnsPolicy is unset.

questions.stem: A Pod uses hostNetwork: true but must resolve cluster Service names. Which dnsPolicy should it set?

options.explanation: Without it, a hostNetwork Pod on ClusterFirst falls back to Default behaviour.
Default inherits node resolution and skips cluster DNS.
None ignores Kubernetes DNS settings entirely.
With hostNetwork, ClusterFirst falls back to Default behaviour.

questions.stem: A Pod sets dnsPolicy: None. Which are true? Select 2.

options.explanation: With None, all DNS settings come from dnsConfig.

options.text: dnsConfig.nameservers must list at least one IP
options.explanation: Required when the policy is None.

options.text: dnsConfig.nameservers can list any number of IPs
options.explanation: At most 3 nameserver IPs are allowed.

options.text: The node's resolv.conf is merged in
options.explanation: None ignores the Kubernetes-provided DNS settings.

questions.stem: A Pod sets hostname: db-0 and subdomain: db in namespace data, but its FQDN doesn't resolve from other Pods. What's most likely missing?

options.text: A headless Service named db in namespace data
options.explanation: DNS serves the Pod's FQDN only if a headless Service with the subdomain's name exists.
That only changes what hostname returns inside the Pod.
The Service must be headless and match the subdomain.
That would stop the Pod using cluster DNS.

questions.stem: Where do you edit the CoreDNS configuration in a typical cluster?

options.explanation: It holds the Corefile.
That's the client side, written by the kubelet.
The Service only exposes CoreDNS; it holds no config.
That configures kube-proxy, not DNS.

questions.stem: All names under consul.local must be answered by a nameserver at a given IP. What do you add to the Corefile?

options.text: A consul.local:53 server block with forward . <nameserver-ip>
options.explanation: That's a stub domain using the forward plugin.

options.text: A cache 30 line in the .:53 block
options.explanation: cache only enables caching.
loadbalance randomizes record order.
That exposes metrics.

questions.stem: Match the default Corefile plugins correctly. Select 3.

options.text: loop: detects simple forwarding loops and halts CoreDNS
options.explanation: Matches the plugin list.

options.text: reload: reloads a changed Corefile automatically
options.explanation: Allow about two minutes after editing.

options.text: kubernetes: answers queries for Services and Pods
options.explanation: It replies based on Service and Pod IPs.

options.text: forward: forwards cluster.local queries to the API server
options.explanation: forward sends queries outside the cluster domain to upstream resolvers.

questions.stem: In clusters running CoreDNS, the DNS Service in kube-system is still named kube-dns.

options.explanation: The name is kept for compatibility with workloads that expect kube-dns.
The CoreDNS Service is named kube-dns.

questions.stem: nslookup kubernetes.default fails from the dnsutils Pod. Which command checks whether the CoreDNS Pods are running?

options.explanation: CoreDNS Pods keep the k8s-app=kube-dns label.
CoreDNS runs in kube-system.
That checks the Service, not the Pods.
That checks CoreDNS's permissions.

questions.stem: CoreDNS Pods run but return SERVFAIL for Service names. Logs suggest it can't read Services. What should you check?

options.text: The system:coredns ClusterRole has list and watch on services and endpointslices
options.explanation: CoreDNS needs these permissions to resolve Service names.

options.text: The kubelet's --cluster-domain flag on every node
options.explanation: That sets Pods' domain; it doesn't grant CoreDNS access.
Queries are reaching CoreDNS; the problem is on its side.

questions.stem: You want CoreDNS to log every query it receives while debugging. What do you do?

options.text: Add the log plugin to the Corefile with kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap coredns
options.explanation: The log plugin records queries; changes reach the Pods within a minute or two.
errors is already in the default Corefile and only logs errors.

options.text: Run kubectl logs on the dnsutils Pod
options.explanation: dnsutils is the client; its logs don't show CoreDNS queries.

questions.stem: When you upgrade a cluster with kubeadm, it can retain your existing CoreDNS Corefile automatically.

options.explanation: kubeadm takes care of keeping the existing CoreDNS configuration.
The page says kubeadm retains it automatically.
